name: ademakov/bzero (hand-written SSE/AVX assembly memset replacements)
baseline: libc memset (README row 'bzero_0: (memset)'; 'stock libc or compiler-provided' memset, version not stated)
workload: Zeroing buffers of 0 to 2048 bytes (sizes 0-17, 31-33, 63-65, ..., 2047-2048), 10,000 calls per size, timed with gettimeofday in main.c; the same harness runs C, intrinsics, rep stosb and hand-written assembly variants against memset.
claimed_speedup: On the i7-4850HQ (README table, microseconds per 10,000 calls, lower is better): 16 B memset=77 vs hand-written SSE assembly bzero_6=32; 64 B 70 vs 26; 256 B 82 vs 51 (about 2.4x, 2.7x and 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Reversed at large sizes: 1024 B memset=149 vs bzero_6=189; 2048 B 241 vs 393. README update says later AVX versions are 'faster than memset() for any memory size' (no table for them).
compiler_and_flags: gcc, version not stated; README says only 'gcc -O2' gives faithful results because gcc -O3 and clang -O2 may rewrite the C versions into memset; Makefile sets CC=gcc, CFLAGS=-march=native.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4850HQ @ 2.30GHz laptop (Haswell, AVX) for the cited numbers; a second table is for an Intel Xeon E5520 @ 2.27GHz (no AVX).
tradeoffs: x86-64 only, AT&T-syntax assembly with SSE or AVX variants (no runtime CPU dispatch in the repo); zeroing only (bzero), not a general memset; the SSE versions lose to stock memset from about 1 KiB upward because glibc uses AVX2 or rep stosb there.
caveats: Hobby experiments on 2013-era CPUs against whatever libc was installed (glibc version not stated); timings are single runs in microseconds with no variance; the headline AVX versions have no numbers in the README, so the cited rows are the SSE bzero_6 variant; the time unit is derived from main.c (gettimeofday microseconds for 10,000 calls) rather than stated in the README; public-domain dedication, no patent grant.
found_via: github.com/topics/simd?l=assembly listing (WebFetch) surfaced ademakov/bzero; opened README.md, main.c, Makefile, LICENSE and commits page. Paper hosts (arXiv, ACM, IEEE) were blocked in this environment.

name: nadavrot/memset_benchmark (AVX2 assembly memset and memcpy)
language: Assembly (x86-64 AVX2, AT&T .S) with C/C++ harness
baseline: glibc memset and memcpy (with and without PLT indirection, 'libc@plt' and 'libc'), also musl and folly (memcpy chart)
workload: README charts: memset and memcpy over random sizes in the 0 to 256 byte range with pre-computed random values (branch mispredictions included, nop-function overhead subtracted), plus per-size sweeps up to 512 bytes; hot-loop single-size charts as well.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'These implementations outperform the folly and glibc implementations.' Random-size chart values (README image, time units not stated, lower is better): memset libc@plt 24344, libc 20172, asm_memset 14295 (about 1.41x faster than libc, derived from chart data); memcpy libc@plt 28285, libc 25263, folly 23969, asm_memcpy 21547 (about 1.17x faster than libc, derived from chart data).
compiler_and_flags: Harness built with CMake: add_compile_options(-Wall -g3 -O3 -march=native) (CMakeLists.txt); the assembly files are not compiler-dependent; glibc version not stated.
stars_or_usage: 344 stars; memset implementation landed in Folly (folly/memset.S) per README
tradeoffs: x86-64 with AVX2 only (vmovdqu/ymm; Apple and Linux symbol variants); tuned for the short-buffer size distribution seen in Chrome, Python and server workloads rather than for large copies; includes exhaustive correctness tester, histogram LD_PRELOAD tool and a proxy tool that swaps builtin memset/memcpy with the local code.
caveats: Results exist only as README images (values read from the chart images); CPU model and glibc version are not stated; repository has no LICENSE file (usability reference; the Folly copy of the memset code is separately licensed Apache-2.0, not verified here); chart numbers come from the author's own run; last commit January 2022.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than glibc" memcpy OR strlen ...' surfaced the HN thread 'A 100LOC C impl of memset, that is faster than glibc's' linking to nadavrot; opened github.com/nadavrot, README.md, docs/*.png, CMakeLists.txt, src/memset/impl.S

name: jnettlet/cortex_a72_memcpy (Cortex-A72 tuned AArch64 memcpy/memset)
baseline: glibc memcpy (the 'memcpy' row) and Arm Optimized Routines memcpy (__memcpy_aarch64, __memcpy_aarch64_simd)
workload: Arm optimized-routines memcpy benchmark on a Cortex-A72: random-size copies from 32K to 1024K, aligned and unaligned medium copies 8 B to 512 B, large copies 1K to 64K, and forwards/backwards unaligned memmove, in bytes per ns.
claimed_speedup: README: 'We are now pretty equivalent or faster than glibc's memcpy and Arm's optimized library memcpy on the optimized library's memcpy benchmark.' Aligned medium memcpy (bytes/ns): 16 B __memcpy_a72 4.40 vs memcpy 2.51; 32 B 8.79 vs 5.03; 64 B 12.80 vs 9.38 (about 1.75x, 1.75x, 1.36x, derived from page data). Random memcpy average 2.01 vs 1.97; large copies equal within 1-2%; unaligned backwards memmove 64K 11.69 vs 6.54.
hardware: Cortex-A72 (board, SoC and clock not stated)
tradeoffs: AArch64 Cortex-A72 only; built as libmemcpy.so for LD_PRELOAD or /etc/ld.so.preload; the stated purpose is fixing copies to memory-mapped device memory (framebuffers, SPDK) by reordering two stores in the 96-byte path, not general speed.
caveats: README tables carry no hardware detail, compiler, flags or method; the 'memcpy' row is presumed to be glibc's; memcpy.S carries an Arm Limited MIT header (Arm optimized-routines lineage; the repo description calls it a patched glibc memcpy), so the speedup is mostly in small aligned sizes (8-64 B) and large/random results are within noise; one row (unaligned 64 B) is slower than libc memcpy (8.46 vs 9.35 bytes/ns).
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than glibc" memcpy OR strlen OR memchr ...' surfaced the repo; opened github.com/jnettlet/cortex_a72_memcpy, README, COPYING and memcpy.S

name: wasi-libc SIMD string routines (opt-in, wasm simd128)
baseline: wasi-libc's own scalar string.h routines (musl-derived SWAR on a 32-bit size_t), i.e. the same library compiled to wasm without -DSIMD=ON
workload: Per-function speedup of wasm simd128 string.h routines (memchr, memcmp, strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp, strncmp, strspn, strcspn, strstr) over the existing implementations when run under the wazero runtime; strlen on 10-byte strings under wasmtime on amd64.
claimed_speedup: ncruces, issue #580 (May 9, 2025), 'rough, only for wazero': memchr 4.3x, memcmp 10.0x, strlen 4.9x, strchr 4.2x, strrchr 9.9x, strcmp 12.8x, strncmp 16.3x, strspn 9.1x, strcspn 9.7x, strstr 5.6x, geomean 7.8x. July 2, 2025: strlen on 10-byte strings under wasmtime on amd64 'still around 2x'.
compiler_and_flags: Built with wasm simd128 (README CMake option -DSIMD=(ON|OFF)); compiler and flags for the benchmark not stated
hardware: Not stated (issue says x86-64 and AArch64 under wazero; wasmtime run on amd64); PR #592 notes a Xeon W-2135 where wasmtime differences were hard to measure
tradeoffs: Opt-in at build time (-DSIMD=ON) and needs a runtime with wasm simd128; functions landed one by one: strlen (#586), memchr (#592), strchrnul (#594), strspn/strcspn (#597), memrchr (#598), memcmp (#603); memchr was switched to inline assembly after an undefined-behaviour concern about pointer arithmetic (#593).
caveats: Numbers are one comment in a tracking issue with no CPU, runtime version, string sizes or harness link ('Numbers are rough, and only for wazero'); a reviewer asked whether the table used 4 MB strings and got no answer; on wasmtime/x86-64 the memchr difference between any_true and bitmask lowering was hard to measure; the speedup baseline is wasm-to-wasm (scalar vs SIMD in the same libc), not native glibc.
found_via: WebSearch 'wasm simd128 strlen memchr strchr musl wasi-libc emscripten faster than scalar string functions pull request benchmark' surfaced wasi-libc PRs #592/#594; opened github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-libc, pull/592, pull/580, issues/580

name: memchr (Rust crate: SIMD memchr, memrchr and memmem)
baseline: libc memmem and libc memchr (system libc called through an FFI engine in the rebar harness; version not stated); README compares against Rust std's substring search
workload: rebar benchmarks recorded 2023-08-26 on x86_64: 54 memmem (substring search across English, Russian, Chinese and subtitle haystacks, never/rare/common needles) and 15 single-byte memchr benchmarks, median per-iteration times.
claimed_speedup: From the recorded CSV (derived from page data, median times): memmem oneshot, crate vs libc memmem, geometric mean 2.00x faster over 54 benchmarks (faster in 41; ranges from libc 2.9x faster to crate 27.8x faster); single-byte memchr oneshot is at parity with libc (geomean 0.94, libc about 6% faster; e.g. sherlock/uncommon/huge1 libc 33.5 us vs crate 57.2 us). README (rebar rank geomean of speed ratios, lower is better, 53 benchmarks): memmem prebuilt crate 1.03 vs std 6.50; oneshot crate 1.04 vs std 5.26.
compiler_and_flags: Engines built with cargo build --release (benchmarks/engines.toml); runtime AVX2 dispatch in the crate; rebar rev 8c6edf6843; Rust toolchain version and libc version not stated in the files opened
tradeoffs: Rust crate with no C API, so not directly linkable from C++; AVX2/SSE2/NEON/wasm32 simd128 with runtime CPU detection and a no_std fallback; the author's argument is that core/libc cannot use AVX without platform-specific dispatch.
caveats: Ratios are derived by the reporter from the recorded CSV; the CSV and the files opened do not name the CPU, libc version or Rust version; first-party harness (rebar) by the crate author; the libc engine is a Rust binary calling libc through FFI, adding call overhead on tiny inputs; single-byte memchr shows no win over libc and the crate is slower on some uncommon-needle cases.
found_via: github.com/topics/memchr page and WebSearch results (rust-memchr PR #35, memchr README); opened README.md, benchmarks/engines.toml and benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv

name: sliceslice (Rust AVX2 substring search)
baseline: Rust std String::find (also memmem, twoway crates and WojciechMula/sse4-strstr in the same table); not libc
workload: Criterion 'i386' benchmark (bench/benches/i386.rs): short haystack: every word of data/words.txt searched in every later word; long haystack: every word searched in data/i386.txt (include_bytes); single-pattern substring search.
claimed_speedup: README table (criterion time, lower is better): short haystack String::find 335.56 ms vs sliceslice DynamicAvx2Searcher 79.416 ms (about 4.2x faster, derived from page data); long haystack 345.01 ms vs 35.181 ms (about 9.8x faster, derived from page data). sse4-strstr avx2_strstr_v2 measures 75.515 ms and 38.579 ms in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.46.0 and gcc 9.3.0; bench/Cargo.toml sets [profile.bench] lto = true, codegen-units = 1; criterion 0.5 harness (bench code in bench/benches/i386.rs)
hardware: HP EliteDesk 800 G2 Tower PC, Intel Core i7-6700 @ 3.40GHz, 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS
tradeoffs: Rust crate (no C API); x86 AVX2 searcher built on Wojciech Mula's SIMD-friendly algorithm with the needle fixed at construction, and unlike sse4-strstr it never reads past the end of the haystack (README footnote).
caveats: Baseline is Rust 1.46 std (2020) String::find, not libc; the memchr crate's own rebar CSV shows sliceslice about 2.06x faster than libc memmem over 39 benchmarks but slower than the memchr crate on 23 of 42 prebuilt comparisons (derived from that CSV); README numbers are from 2020 toolchains.
found_via: WebSearch 'SIMD-friendly substring search strstr memmem AVX2 SSE4.2 speedup over glibc github' surfaced cloudflare/sliceslice-rs; opened README.md, bench/Cargo.toml, bench/benches/i386.rs

name: FastMemcpy (skywind3000)
baseline: 'traditional memcpy' in gcc 4.9 and MSVC 2012 (C runtime memcpy; glibc not named)
workload: memcpy of 32 B to 8 MiB buffers with aligned and unaligned source and destination (16.7M iterations at 32 B down to 256 at 8 MiB) plus a random-access copy benchmark, wall time in ms.
claimed_speedup: README: '50% speedup in avg. vs traditional memcpy in msvc 2012 or gcc 4.9'. gcc 4.9 rows: 32 B both aligned memcpy_fast=81ms vs memcpy=281 ms; 64 B 91ms vs 364 ms; 4 MiB 263ms vs 398 ms; random access 487ms vs 1000ms. Counter-example in the same table: 1 MiB both aligned memcpy_fast=181ms vs memcpy=165 ms.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9 (MSVC 2012 'got a similar result'); build lines gcc -O3 -msse2 FastMemcpy.c and gcc -O3 -mavx FastMemcpy_Avx.c, MSVC -O2; the flags used for the tables are not stated
tradeoffs: x86 SSE2 or AVX only; jump table for small sizes, SSE2 vector copy for medium, cache prefetch plus non-temporal movntdq stores for huge sizes; README says the block-prefetch method covers only aligned huge copies and other cases are left to the user; plain memcpy (non-overlapping) semantics.
caveats: 2017 results against 2014-era gcc 4.9 and MSVC 2012 runtime memcpy, before modern ERMS/FSRM-aware glibc dispatch; CPU, OS, libc and timing method are not stated; the average claim is not supported by every row (1 MiB aligned is slower than memcpy); the non-temporal stores can hurt when the destination is read right after.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/skywind3000/FastMemcpy during the memcpy discovery pass (WebSearch 'github fast memcpy memmove memset AVX2 AVX-512 faster than glibc'); opened README.md and LICENSE

name: AOCL-LibMem (AMD optimized memory and string functions)
baseline: glibc memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp, memchr, strcpy, strncpy, strcmp, strncmp, strlen, strnlen, strcat, strncat, strstr, strspn, strchr (benchmark tool compares against the glibc installed on the test host)
workload: No results published. The repo ships a benchmark framework (TinyMemBench, Google Benchmark hot/cold cache, Google FleetBench v0.2 and v0.3.3, Meta DCPerf) that reports throughput gain in percent of LibMem over host glibc for memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: library 'highly optimized for AMD Zen micro-architecture' with multiple implementations per function chosen at runtime; benchmark_guide.md: 'Gives the Throughput gains in %age' against glibc.
compiler_and_flags: AOCC or GCC per the benchmark guide; CMake flag ALMEM_ARCH selects AVX2 or AVX512 builds; no benchmark flags stated
hardware: AMD Zen microarchitecture (AVX2 or AVX-512 builds)
stars_or_usage: 38 stars; AMD's official AOCL component (releases 5.0 to 5.3.2)
tradeoffs: Tuned for AMD Zen and Linux only; loading the AVX512 build on a CPU without AVX-512 crashes; small sizes use page-boundary-safe unmasked vector loads like glibc, with an ALMEM_STRICT_BOUNDS=Y masked-load variant; IFUNC and glibc 2.34+ dlopen symbol caveats; includes third-party tinymembench (MIT).
caveats: Tier D: no published numbers anywhere in the repo pages opened (README, benchmark guide, user guide); amd.com product page was unreachable here; the benchmark tool exists so claims are checkable by running it on Zen hardware.
found_via: WebSearch 'vectorized libc string functions memcpy strlen strcmp AVX-512 SVE paper evaluation speedup over glibc musl' surfaced AOCL-LibMem; opened github.com/amd/aocl-libmem, README, LICENSE, benchmark_guide.md, User_Guide.md

name: mysterywolf/rt_memcpy_cm (Cortex-M LDM/STM assembly memcpy)
baseline: Keil C library memcpy and RT-Thread's C rt_memcpy
workload: Copying 10000 bytes, 10000 times, in the Keil environment.
claimed_speedup: README (Chinese): Keil, 10000 bytes copied 10000 times: rt_memcpy 1261 ms, this assembly version 883 ms, C library memcpy 906 ms (about 1.43x faster than rt_memcpy and 1.03x faster than the C library, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Keil (version and optimisation level not stated); ports exist for Keil, GCC and IAR
hardware: Cortex-M3/M4/M7 (exact MCU and clock not stated)
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; published as an RT-Thread online package
tradeoffs: Cortex-M3/4/7 only; speed comes from LDMIA/STMIA moving up to 40 bytes per instruction pair; handles addresses that are not 4-byte aligned; shipped for the RT-Thread ecosystem.
caveats: The win over the C library is about 3% and the README does not give MCU, compiler version or flags; README says the assembly originates from Silicon Labs (uC/OS), so provenance of the code versus the repo's Apache-2.0 LICENSE file is not verified; the large gain is against RT-Thread's own C rt_memcpy.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/topics/memcpy?l=assembly (memcpy discovery pass); opened the repo page, README.md, LICENSE and commits page

name: charltoncr/strstr.c (public-domain strstr)
baseline: C standard library strstr implementations (the 18 competitors in Competitors/strstrFunctions.c include 4.4BSD (Chris Torek), Microsoft and GNU coreutils 5.3.0 versions)
workload: Finding English words in English text with a 15-line scalar strstr compared with 18 diverse strstr implementations.
claimed_speedup: README: 'tied for speed with its nearest competitor among 18 diverse strstr implementations when finding English words in English text'; 'Its other competitors are between 10.5% and 348% slower'; 15 executable lines versus 67 for the nearest competitor.
tradeoffs: Plain scalar C (no SIMD or assembly), a strchr-like unrolled first-character scan then naive compare, so worst case is O(n*m); drop-in strstr semantics.
caveats: Only relative percentages are given; the timing harness and raw results are not in the repo (Competitors/ holds only strstrFunctions.c); competitors are classic public implementations, not current glibc or musl strstr (two-way, SSE); CPU, compiler and flags unstated; CC0 gives no patent grant.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/topics/strstr (discovery pass); opened README.md, LICENSE.md, Competitors/strstrFunctions.c and commits page
